title: Impact of RAS-MAPK Pathway Genetic Alterations on Radiotherapy Response in Metastatic Lung Adenocarcinoma
author: Gustav Y Cederquist; Erik S Anderson; Eric Lis; Lily Boe; William C Newman; Ori Barzilai; Mark Bilsky; Yoshiya Yamada; Daniel S Higginson; Adam M Schmitt
text:
Abstract
Purpose:
To determine whether driver gene alterations in metastatic non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) spine metastases are associated with local tumor control after radiotherapy.
Patients and Methods:
Patients with NSCLC who underwent radiotherapy (RT) for spine metastasis and tumor genetic profiling were ascertained. Associations between driver gene mutations incidence of local failure were analyzed, followed by competing risk analysis for significant associations. Results were validated using in vitro clonal survival assays of CRISPR-engineered NSCLC cell lines.
Results:
181 patients were analyzed with median follow up was 15.2 months (IQR 8.0 – 31.9 months). The 3-year risk of local failure was 0.15 (95% CI 0.10 – 0.20). Patients harboring NF1 or BRAF driver alterations experienced higher 3-year local failure rates (NF1: 0.33 (0.09–0.61) vs. 0.13 (0.09 – 0.19), p = 0.002); BRAF: 0.31 (0.08–0.57) vs. 0.13 (0.09–0.19), p = 0.04). NF1 loss-of-function mutations conferred radio-resistance in one of two NSCLC cell lines tested in vitro. Based on the convergence of NF1 and BRAF signaling, the RAS-MAPK pathway was further interrogated. KRAS mutations overall were not associated local failure. However, co-mutation of KRAS/TP53 exhibited a trend toward elevated 3-year local failure, 0.31 (0.11–0.55) vs. 0.13 (0.08 vs. 0.19), p = 0.05. RAS-MAPK pathway driver alterations accounted for 53% of all local failures (p<0.0001), and showed an elevated 3-year risk of local failure (0.36 (0.2 – 0.51) vs. 0.09 (0.05 – 0.15), p < 0.001), including when treated with stereotactic body radiotherapy (0.28 (0.1 – 0.5) vs. 0.05 (0.02 – 0.11), p = 0.001).
Conclusion:
Driver alterations in the RAS-MAPK signaling pathway confer radio-resistance in metastatic NSCLC. These genetic alterations may serve as biomarkers to personalize RT strategies or as targets to enhance radiosensitivity.
Introduction:
Radiotherapy is increasingly being used to treat metastatic disease. It is used to control local tumor growth and protect surrounding normal tissue. Radiotherapy is also used to provide systemic disease control in the oligometastatic state. For example, radiotherapy is a primary treatment modality for spine metastases 1, which if allowed to grow unrestrained could threaten the integrity of the spinal cord. Randomized data support the use of radiotherapy for the treatment of oligometastatic disease across a number of tumor types, demonstrating improved outcomes including superior survival2–6. However, optimal patient selection for metastasis-directed therapy remains unclear. Identifying genetic biomarkers of radiosensitivity in metastatic disease will help to define the optimal use of radiotherapy in the oligo- and polymetastatic setting.
Here, we search for genetic associations of radiosensitivity in metastatic tumors, focusing on non-small cell lung adenocarcinoma (NSCLC) spine metastases. This approach has three main advantages. First, limiting analysis to spine metastasis controls for the impact of local tumor microenvironment on treatment response. Second, there are known genetic alterations associated with local tumor control in localized NSCLC, which include STK11 7, KEAP1/NRF28, NFE2L2 9, and PIK3CA10; this should provide insight into differences between tumor biology in the localized and metastatic setting. Third, radiotherapy has proven benefit in the treatment of oligometastatic NSCLC 2, 3, and elucidating genetic alterations associated with radiation response may have direct clinical implication as biomarkers for personalization of treatment.
We assembled a cohort of NSCLC patients with spine metastasis treated with radiotherapy and who underwent tumor genomic profiling to identify driver gene mutations that are associated local failure. Validation was performed using in vitro clonal survival assays and immunofluorescence with CRISPR-engineered cell lines. Our results implicate genetic alteration of the RAS-MAPK pathway as a common driver pathway of radio-resistance in metastatic NSCLC.
Methods:
NSCLC spine metastasis patients and radiation treatment:
We retrospectively assessed consecutive patients with NSCLC and spine metastasis treated with external beam radiotherapy between December 2009 – May 2018. Evaluated patients gave informed consent and underwent targeted next generation sequencing 11. Next generation sequencing was performed on primary or metastatic tissue samples. This research was conducted in accordance with the US Common rule, and this study was approved by the Institutional Review Board.
Standard pre-treatment evaluation included a physical exam and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the total spine, or in a small number of cases computed tomography (CT) scan of the spine. Radiotherapy dosing was divided into conventional external beam radiotherapy (cEBRT) including doses of 800cGy/1 fraction, 1600cGy/4 fractions, 2000cGy/5 fractions, 2500cGy/5 fractions and 3000cGy/10 fractions, and stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SBRT) including doses of 3000cGy/5 fractions, 2400cGy/3 fractions, 2700cGy/3 fractions, 3000cGy/3 fractions, 2400cGy/1 fraction. Treatment technique included 3D conformal radiotherapy (3D-CRT) and SBRT. SBRT treatment planning included a CT myelogram prior to simulation or high-resolution volumetric MRI for image fusion. In general, imaging with MRI or CT was performed every 6 months post treatment. Local failure was assessed by a blinded expert neuroradiologist.
Tumor genomic profiling and driver gene mutations:
Each patient underwent tumor genomic profiling using Memorial Sloan Kettering Next Generation Sequencing Platforms (NGS). 180/181 patients had available genetic data from the IMPACT tumor sequencing platform (versions 3–7) 12. Additionally, 9/181 patients had available genetic data from the ACCESS cell-free DNA sequencing platform 13. 1 patient had ACCESS but no available IMPACT data at the time of analysis. Driver gene mutations were defined for each patient using cBioPortal and were limited to with greater than 5% frequency in the cohort. Samples were pooled when patients had multiple NGS samples. All driver mutations except CDKN2A were included in all versions of the IMPACT gene panel. All driver mutations except MDM2 and NKX2–1 were included in the ACCESS gene panel. A KEAP1/STK11/NFE2L2/PIC3KA (KSNP) group was assembled, which includes all patients with driver mutations in the aforementioned four. A DNA Damage response (DDR) group was assembled, which includes all patients with driver mutations in a 43 gene panel comprising DNA damage and response pathways 14. Patient level data is provided (Table S1 and Table S2)
NSCLC cell lines:
The H2126 (human male NSCLC, metastatic pleural effusion origin, acquired from ATCC) was maintained in DMEM:F12 (MSKCC media core) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (VWR, 97068–085) + 1x pen/strep (MSKCC media core). The H1299 cell line (human male NSCLC, metastatic lymph node origin, acquired from ATCC) was maintained in RPMI 1640 (MSKCC media core) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (VWR, 97068–085) + 1x pen/strep (MSKCC media core). Cultures were passaged with 0.05% Trypsin-EDTA (MSKCC media core) and maintained at 37°C in a humidified 5% CO2 atmosphere.
CRISPR-based genetic modification of NSCLC cell lines:
NF1 frameshift mutations were introduced using sgRNAs targeting the NF1 locus. For the H2126 line, sgRNAs were constructed in a pSico constitutive expression plasmid which also contains mCherry and puromycin resistance genes (Addgene, 51024). gRNA-A sequence: GGTTACCTGCTCGTCGAAG; gRNA-B sequence: GGAGGACATGGCCGCGCAC. sgRNA plasmids were co-transfected with the px330 plasmid expressing Cas9 using lipofectamine 3000. 48 hours later, transfected cells were selected using 2ng/mL puromycin for 72 hours. For the H1299 line, the Origene human gene knockout CRISPR Kit (Origene, KN420378) was used according to the manufacturer protocol. Individual clones were then isolated and sequenced by subcloning and sanger sequencing, as above. All subclones were verified to be frameshift indels, or large insertions and deletions.
Clonal survival assays
Cells were passaged and plated at 60–70% confluency. On the next day cells were irradiated with doses of 0Gy, 2Gy, 4Gy, and 6Gy. After 1 hour cells were trypsinized and plated at clonal density. Clones were then grown for 14 to 21 days until colonies were visible and fixed with 100% Methanol (Fisher, A412P-4) for 20 minutes. Fixed colonies were stained with cresyl violet for 45 to 60 minutes and wished with sterile dH2O. Plates were imaged using GelCount Cell Colony Counter (Oxford Optronix), and colonies were counted using the “analyze particles” function of FIJI image analysis software. Uniform threshold and size criteria were used within each experiment for colony counting. Survival curves were generated using Graphpad Prism software.
γH2AX Foci analysis
Cells were passaged and plated at 60–70% confluency and irradiated on the following day at a dose of 4Gy. Cells were plated onto circular cover glass (Electron Microscopy, 72230–01). Cells were fixed at four time points: prior to radiation, 1 hour post, 4 hours post, 24 hours post radiation. Cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (Fisher, AA433689M) in 1x phosphate buffered saline (PBS, MSKCC Media core) for 20 minutes. After three 10 minutes washes with PBS, cells were blocked with 10% normal donkey serum in PBS (Jackson Immunoresearch, 017-00-121) for 30 minutes, incubated with primary antibody at 4°C overnight. γH2AX antibody (Millipore, 05–636) was diluted 1:1200 in 1% bovine serum albumin (Thermo Fisher, AM2616) in PBS-T (PBS with 0.1% Triton X-100). The next day, cells were washed three times for 10 minutes in PBS-T, cells were incubated with secondary fluorescent antibody for 1 hour. Anti-mouse 594 and 680 secondary antibodies (Alexa series, ThermoFisher, A11004, A21057) were diluted 1:1000 in PBS-T. Cells were then incubated with DAPI, diluted 1:5000 in PBS, for 10 minutes. Cells were washed three times for 10 minutes with PBS and mounted onto glass slides (ThermoFisher, 12-550-15) using ProLong Gold Antifade Media (Fisher Scientific, P10144). Images were obtained using a Zeiss LSM 880 confocal laser scanning microscope and analyzed using ImageJ (https://microscopy.duke.edu/guides/count-nuclear-foci-ImageJ).
Statistical analysis
To identify candidate genes that are associated with radio-resistance, hazard ratio of local failure was calculated for each gene. The associated p-values were calculated. The associated false discovery rate q values were calculated using the Benjamini-Yekutieli method to account for multiple comparisons. Cumulative incidence risk of local failure were calculated with death as a competing risk 15. Data were censored at the end of July 2020 when the final local failure analysis was performed. Differences in survival clonal fraction were calculated using ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s test to account for multiple comparisons. Unless otherwise stated, 95% confidence intervals are reported with all cumulative risk estimates.
Results:
Characteristics of NSCLC spine metastasis patients treated with radiotherapy
We identified 181 consecutive patients and 264 samples with NSCLC who received radiotherapy for spine metastasis and who had tumor genomic profiling on primary or metastatic tissue biopsies. Median follow up was 15.2 months (IQR 8.0 – 31.9). Median age was 61.5 years (IQR 54.2 – 70.5) and was 65% females and 35% males. The thoracic spine was the most common site of treatment (43.3%) (Table 1). All spine tumors were metastatic lesions as opposed to local progression of primary lung tumors. 43% of patients were treated with cEBRT (78/181) and 57% of patients were treated with SBRT (103/181). 41% of samples were from the primary tumor (106/264) and 57% of samples were from a metastatic site (150/264).

Overall treatment outcomes
Among all patients treated with spine radiotherapy, median overall survival from the time of radiotherapy was 16.0 months (Table S3). The incidence of local failure was 16.6% (30/181) within the follow up period. The 3-year risk of local failure was 0.15 (0.10 – 0.20) (Fig 1A), and the 3-year risk of failure at an adjacent (out-of-field) vertebral site was 0.17 (0.12 – 0.22) (Fig S1A, Table S1). The 3-year estimated risk of local failure with SBRT vs. cEBRT was 0.09 (0.04 – 0.16) vs. 0.22 (0.13–0.32), p = 0.03 (Fig 1B).
Genetic associations with local failure
There were 21 driver alterations within the NGS panel with frequency of greater than 5% (Table 2). Patients with driver mutations in the genes NF1 (Hazard Ratio (HR) 4.7), BRAF (HR 2.9), MYC (HR 3.6), and CDK4 (HR 2.7) had a significantly elevated risk of local failure, and NF1 maintained significance after multiple comparison testing (q = 0.007) (Table 2).

The estimated 3-year risk of local failure in patients with NF1 mutations was 0.33 (0.09–0.61) vs. 0.13 (0.09 – 0.19) in non-carriers (p = 0.002) (Fig 1C). NF1 driver alterations were associated with local failure for cEBRT (p = 0.007) but not SBRT (p = 0.06) (Fig S1B). The estimated 3-year risk of local failure in patients with BRAF mutations was 0.31 (0.08–0.57) vs. 0.13 (0.09–0.19) in non-carriers (p = 0.040) (Fig 1D). BRAF was also associated with increased risk of local failure in patients treated with cEBRT (p = 0.04), but not SBRT (Fig S1C). KEAP1, STK11, NFEL2, and PIK3CA (KSNP) mutations have been associated with radio-resistance for primary lung tumors 7–10, 14. In combination, these genes showed a non-significant trend toward elevated risk of local failure (Fig S1D).
NF1 confers radio-resistance
To validate these findings we engineered the H2126 NSCLC line to harbor an NF1 mutation. The H2126 cell line is not known to harbor mutations in NF1, BRAF, KRAS, NRAS, or HRAS (Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia). Two independent guide RNAs (A and B) were used. Both H2126 lines demonstrated a radio-resistant phenotype (Fig 2A,B). At 6Gy, the average surviving fraction of the parent line was 0.0086, while the average surviving fractions of the NF1 A.3 and NF1 B.7 lines were 0.11 and 0.058 respectively (One-way ANOVA p < 0.0001, Parent vs. A.3 p < 0.0001, Parent vs. B.7 p = 0.0015, p values corrected using Dunnett Test).
The NF1 radio-resistance phenotype was not seen in the H1299 line (Fig S2). Interestingly, the H1299 parent line harbors an NRAS Q61K driver alteration, which may mask the effect of NF1 loss-of-function. These data provide experimental evidence supporting the association of NF1 driver alterations with radio-resistance in NSCLC.
DNA double strand break repair kinetics are not altered in NF1 mutant cell lines
Induction of DNA damage via double strand breaks is a primary mechanism of radiation-induced cell injury. To test the hypothesis that NF1 alters radiosensitivity via changes in DNA-Damage Response (DDR), we measured the kinetics of double strand break generation and repair by monitoring a time course of γH2AX phosphorylation after cell irradiation at 4Gy. Overall, this analysis revealed that the kinetics of γH2AX foci generation and resolution at 1, 4, or 24 hours after irradiation were similar between parent and NF1 mutant lines (Fig 3A). DDR mutations were not associated with altered radiosensitivity (Fig 3B), unlike in the primary tumor site14.
KRAS/TP53 mutations are associated with increased local failure
In vitro studies did not support the hypothesis that NF1 reduced radiosensitivity via alterations to DDR signaling. We therefore tested a second hypothesis that NF1 confers radio-resistance via altered RAS-MAPK pathway signaling. To explore this pathway we analyzed rates of local failure associated with KRAS mutations. Overall, KRAS mutations do not alter the risk local failure (Fig 4A, Table 2). However, the effect of KRAS on oncogenesis is context dependent. In the absence of TP53 co-mutation KRAS induces senescence, while in the presence of TP53 co-mutation it acts as an oncogene 16. This behavior is dependent on MAPK signaling 17. Therefore, we analyzed local failure rates among patients harboring KRAS/TP53 co-mutations. Patients with MDM2 amplifications were also included based on its known direct regulation of P53. KRAS/TP53 pathway carriers exhibited a trend toward increased local failure risk at 3 years 0.31 (0.11–0.55) vs. 0.17 (0.11 vs. 0.25) in non-carriers, p = 0.05 (Fig 4B).
Local failure is frequently associated with RAS-MAPK pathway alterations
Among the 30 failure events in overall cohort, 53% of patients (16/30) had an alteration in the RAS-MAPK pathway defined as NF1, BRAF, and KRAS/TP53 pathway alterations (p = 0.0001 by chi squared). In our cohort patients rarely harbored more than one RAS-MAPK alteration, suggesting these variants function in a common genetic pathway. To confirm this, we used cBioPortal to analyze a larger cohort of NSCLC patients and verified mutual exclusivity of RAS-MAPK alterations (Fig 4C, Fig S3A). In the combined analysis, the 3-year risk of local failure with any RAS-MAPK driver alteration was 0.36 (0.2 – 0.51) vs. 0.09 (0.05 – 0.15) in non-carriers (p < 0.001). RAS-MAPK pathway alterations were also associated with a higher 3-year risk of local failure after cEBRT (0.44 (0.19–0.66) vs. 0.15 (0.07–0.26), p < 0.001) and SBRT (0.28 (0.10 – 0.5) vs. 0.05 (0.02 – 0.11), p = 0.0008) (Fig S3B). Overall progression free survival (PFS) from the time of radiotherapy was not different between RAS-MAPK pathway carriers and non-carriers (Fig S3C).
Discussion:
We show that driver alterations of RAS-MAPK signaling are associated with radio-resistance in metastatic NSCLC. We retrospectively analyzed 181 patients treated with radiotherapy for NSCLC spine metastases and identified NF1, BRAF, and KRAS/TP53 pathway driver alterations are associated with an elevated risk of local failure. In total these convergent RAS-MAPK pathway alterations accounted for 20% of the entire cohort, 53% of all failures, and were associated with local failure after SBRT. In vitro clonal survival assays showed that NF1 loss-of-function conferred radio-resistance, validating the clinical observations. This phenotype was observed in two independent clones of the H2126 line. Interestingly, the H1299 cell line, in which NF1 did not confer radio-resistance, harbors an NRAS Q61K driver alteration, which may mask the impact of an NF1 mutation.
The association of RAS alterations and radio-resistance were first demonstrated at least 3 decades ago18, 19. Various mechanisms have been proposed for RAS mediated radio-resistance including alterations in cell cycle progression 20, DNA Damage Response 21, and PI3K signaling 22–24. While some studies suggest that MAPK signaling is not responsible for RAS dependent radio-resistance 24, other studies have shown than inhibition of the RAF-MEK-ERK signaling with small molecules sensitizes cells to radiation 25–28. Concurrent delivery of RAF or MEK inhibitors with radiotherapy increases treatment toxicity, providing clinical evidence that the MAPK pathway alters radiosensitivity 25, 29–33; consensus guidelines recommend against concurrent BRAF inhibitor and radiotherapy due to increased normal tissue toxicity 34. Together, these data strongly suggest that RAS-MAPK signaling modulates radiation sensitivity, but impact may be context dependent.
NF1 has not been associated in increased local failure rates after radiotherapy to our knowledge, however tumors with NF1 mutations have been shown to exhibit an increased rate of secondary malignancy after radiotherapy. Mice harboring NF1 mutant alleles develop in field solid tumors such as sarcomas and myeloid malignancies at a higher rate than wild type counterparts35, 36. The association of NF1 mutations and increased risk of secondary malignant neoplasm after radiotherapy has been validated in human cohorts with long term follow up 37. The precise mechanism of radiation induced secondary malignant neoplasm in NF1 mutant tumors is unknown, but may be related to a differing patterns of genetic alterations after radiotherapy 38.
There are at least two major limitations of our study. First, our study did not formally evaluate the effect of systemic therapy on local control of metastatic spine tumors. It is possible patients in the non-RAS-MAPK cohort were more likely to targetable mutations such as EGFR, and this impacted local control 39. While this is formally possible, EGFR carriers did not exhibit improved local. Furthermore, there was no difference in overall PFS in the RAS-MAPK carriers versus non-carriers suggesting that systemic therapy response was not the main driver behind local tumor control. Second, tumor sequencing analysis was not restricted to the irradiated lesion. All available sequencing data from primary sites, metastatic sites, and blood were pooled for each patient. Prior work has shown that there is in fact a high concordance of mutations across primary and metastatic tumor sites within a single patient, supporting our approach 40.
In summary, our data provide evidence that driver alterations in the RAS-MAPK pathway confer radio-resistance to NSCLC spine metastases and implicate the RAS-MAPK pathway as a genetic biomarker to guide radiotherapy in metastatic NSCLC. Given the inferior local control in patients with RAS-MAPK pathway alterations, the use of SBRT in this population is especially important when feasible. More broadly, randomized clinical trials now support an emerging paradigm that treating all sites of oligometastatic disease with SBRT can improve progression free and overall survival 2, 5. Effective translation of this strategy into widespread clinical practice will require careful patient selection; RAS-MAPK pathway alterations could potentially be used to select patients who will durably respond to comprehensive SBRT for oligometastatic NSCLC. Finally, it will be interesting to explore whether pharmacologic targeting of RAS-MAPK signaling could be a viable strategy for radio-sensitization in metastatic NSCLC.

Context Summary.
Key Objective:
To explore the association between driver gene alterations and local tumor control after spine radiotherapy for metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
Knowledge Generated:
This work identifies convergent driver gene alterations in the RAS-MAPK signaling pathway that are associated with reduced local tumor control after radiotherapy for metastatic NSCLC. NF1 loss-of-function mutations were introduced into NSCLC cell lines using CRISPR-based gene editing and conferred in vitro radioresistance.
Relevance:
These data identify potential genetic biomarkers to inform personalized delivery of radiotherapy for patients with oligo and poly-metastatic NSCLC.
